bind joins a queue to a RabbitExchange under a routing key; a direct exchange routes on the exact key, and the default exchange on queue names. A publisher sends a message to an exchange, never to a queue. The exchange copies the message into the queues bound to it whose bindings match. RabbitExchange names the exchange of a binding, and its constructor names its type: Constructor Routes on direct the exact routing key topic a dotted pattern of the routing key fanout nothing: every bound queue gets every message headers the message's headers, against the binding's arguments consistent_hash a hash of the routing key, through a plugin bind(exchange, routing_key) adds a binding to a queue descriptor, and a queue may carry several. A direct exchange delivers a message to every queue bound under its routing key exactly; a message under a key no queue is bound under goes nowhere. The default exchange, with the empty name, is a direct exchange every queue is bound to under its own name. So a message published with no exchange reaches the queue its routing key names, and a binding to the default exchange is refused. An exchange is durable by default and survives a broker restart, and auto_delete is off. The exchange and its bindings reach the server when the broker declares the topology; the built-in amq.* exchanges are bound to and never declared. The publishing side names its exchange on the publish policy with exchange, and the message's name is its routing key. RabbitExchange::custom(name, kind) names an exchange of a type a server plugin provides, such as x-random or x-modulus-hash. A queue binds to it with bind, or with bind_with for a plugin that routes on binding arguments. The plugin does the routing, so the server needs the plugin enabled, and the in-process transport routes nothing through such an exchange.

Checkout publishes each payment to the direct exchange payments under its method; the card queue is bound under card, the invoice queue under invoice. bind_with binds a queue to a headers exchange by x-match and the headers to match, all of them or any one. A headers exchange ignores the routing key and routes on the message's headers. bind_with(exchange, routing_key, arguments) gives the binding an argument table, a FieldTable of AMQPValue entries. The entry x-match decides the rule: all takes a message that carries every other entry of the table with the same value, and any takes a message that carries at least one. The other entries are the headers to match, and the routing key of the binding is usually empty. A plain bind to a headers exchange sends an empty table, and all of no headers is true of every message, so such a queue gets everything the exchange gets. The publishing side sets the headers on the message, and they ride the AMQP header table the exchange reads. bind_with also serves a plugin exchange that routes on binding arguments.

consistent_hash spreads a stream over queues bound with integer weights, by a hash of the routing key, through the RabbitMQ plugin. The constructor exists with the crate's plugin-consistent-hash feature and names the x-consistent-hash type of the rabbitmq_consistent_hash_exchange plugin. The server needs the plugin enabled: rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_consistent_hash_exchange. Each queue binds with its weight as the routing key, such as "1" or "2", and takes that share of the hash space. The exchange hashes the routing key of each message, so messages with one key always reach the same queue. So a key such as a customer or an account keeps its messages in one queue, in order, while the stream spreads over all of them. Within one service instance, lanes give the same per-key order without the plugin. The plugin does the routing on the server. The in-process transport declares the exchange and its bindings and routes nothing through it, so a test of the spread runs against a plugin-enabled server with TestApp::start_live.

Orders are hashed by customer over two shards of equal weight. A fanout exchange copies every message to every bound queue and ignores the routing key. A queue binds to a fanout exchange with any routing key, usually the empty one. Each bound queue gets its own copy, and each copy is consumed and settled on its own. So a fanout exchange is the broadcast of RabbitMQ: one event, many independent consumers. A service that needs a copy in every instance binds an exclusive queue per instance.

A price change reaches both the search index and the cache, each through a queue of its own. A topic exchange routes on dotted routing-key patterns, where * matches one word and # any number of words. A routing key of a topic exchange is a list of words separated by dots, such as order.created or order.shipped.late. A queue binds with a pattern of the same shape. * stands for exactly one word, and # for zero or more words. So order.* takes order.created and passes order.shipped.late by, and order.# takes both. A pattern without wildcards matches its key exactly, as on a direct exchange. A message that matches several bindings of one queue reaches that queue once. A handler that serves several keys reads the key of each delivery through the RoutingKey context key.

LapinPublish, Publish in the prelude, is the fire-and-forget publish policy: a publish resolves once the frame is written, with no broker confirm. The message name is the routing key, and the exchange belongs to the policy. By default that is the default exchange, where a routing key addresses the queue of the same name; exchange names another. The policy holds no connection. At startup the runtime pairs it with the connected broker into a LapinPublisher, which publishes on the connection's shared publish channel. A publisher kept past shutdown answers every publish with AmqpError::Closed. A mount site names the policy wherever a registration publishes: .out_reply(Publish::default()) for a reply, .out(Slot, Publish::default()) for a slot. It is also the broker's default policy, so a registration that names none replies through it. Where a reply goes is a property of the reply type, as the core's replies page describes. A publish outside a handler goes through after_startup on the broker scope: once the subscriptions are open, the runtime pairs the policy and hands the hook the live publisher. The policy holds the defaults of the per-message properties. confirms and server_tx move to the transactional policies and keep these settings. Automatic recovery restores publisher channels and confirms, but does not replay failed publishes. A publish during an outage can return an error, and the outcome of an in-flight publish can be uncertain. An application that retries must account for possible duplicates. Connection readiness alone does not mean every publisher channel has finished recovering. A recovered publisher channel can also precede binding restoration on another channel; a confirmed publish can then be unroutable and discarded, as described under connection recovery.

Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name the reply type declares. Once its subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. Macros Manual examples/lapin_publishing_publish.rs /// Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name its type declares. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish::default()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".into(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_publish.rs /// Every order is answered with a confirmation, routed under the name its type declares. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let confirm = subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Confirm); b.include(confirm.reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the service announces itself. b.after_startup(Publish::default(), async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "orders".into(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) }

exchange sends a policy's publishes to a named exchange instead of the default exchange. The message name stays the routing key, and the exchange routes by it. A topic exchange matches it against binding patterns, a direct exchange matches it exactly, and a fanout exchange ignores it. Without exchange, the default exchange delivers to the queue whose name equals the routing key. RabbitMQ accepts a publish that matches no binding and drops it. Every publish policy of the crate takes the setting: ConfirmsPublish, ServerTxPublish and LapinRequest too. With declare_topology(true), the subscription that binds a queue to the exchange declares the exchange.

Every accepted order is announced on the events topic exchange under order.placed. An audit queue bound under order.* receives it. b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Accept).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default().exchange("events")) .build(); b.include(subscriber(audit, Audit).build()); }) }

A publish's headers travel in the AMQP frame: content-type, correlation-id, reply-to and message-id ride the native properties of those names, and every other header lands in the header table. A handler hands the headers to the publish builder with .with_headers(..), as a HeaderMap or as the typed contract its message declares. The four identity headers become properties, so a consumer written against another client finds them where the protocol puts them. Every other header is a byte string in the header table, so a binary value survives the round trip. A delivery reports both kinds back as headers, and the handler reads them from its context. A header another client or the server wrote with a typed value arrives too: a boolean as true or false, an integer or a timestamp in decimal, a float as its shortest decimal, an AMQP decimal with its scale applied (19.99), and an array or a table as compact JSON with a table's fields in name order. So the server's x-death record reads as [{"count":1,"exchange":"","queue":"orders","reason":"rejected",...}]. The text keeps the value and not its AMQP type, so a header this service publishes again travels as a string. A delivery also reports two properties under headers of their own: the priority under PRIORITY_HEADER (amqp-priority) and the TTL under EXPIRATION_HEADER (amqp-expiration). A header never sets a delivery property: priority, expiration and delivery mode are properties of the policy and the publish builder. An AMQP property is a short string of at most 255 bytes, and a longer identity header fails the publish with AmqpError::InvalidOptions before anything is routed.

The invoice carries the order's reference as its message-id property and the tenant in the header table. The billing side reads both from its context. Macros Manual examples/lapin_publishing_headers.rs /// The invoice carries the order's reference as its `message-id` property and the tenant in the /// header table. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn issue_invoice(order: &Order, Out(invoices): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("message-id", order.reference.clone()); headers.insert("tenant", "acme"); let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id }; if let Err(err) = invoices .message(&invoice) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { // A reference longer than a short string is refused, and a retry will not shorten it. tracing::error!(order.id, %err, "invoice refused"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The billing side reads both where it reads every header. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("invoices"))] async fn bill(invoice: &Invoice, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let reference = ctx.headers().get_str("message-id").unwrap_or_default(); let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(invoice.order_id, reference, tenant, "invoice billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(issue_invoice) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include(bill); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_publishing_headers.rs /// The invoice carries the order's reference as its `message-id` property and the tenant in the /// header table. struct IssueInvoice; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for IssueInvoice where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("message-id", order.reference.clone()); headers.insert("tenant", "acme"); let invoice = Invoice { order_id: order.id }; let invoices = outs.get(DefaultSlot); if let Err(err) = invoices .message(&invoice) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await { // A reference longer than a short string is refused, and a retry will not shorten it. tracing::error!(order.id, %err, "invoice refused"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(()) } } /// The billing side reads both where it reads every header. struct Bill; impl Handle<Invoice> for Bill { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let reference = ctx.headers().get_str("message-id").unwrap_or_default(); let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant").unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(invoice.order_id, reference, tenant, "invoice billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), IssueInvoice).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish::default()) .build(); b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("invoices"), Bill).build()); }, ) }

LapinPublishSteps adds priority, expiration and persistent to the publish builder, so a handler sets an AMQP property of one message. A publish policy holds the defaults for every message it sends, and a step adjusts one message over them. LapinPublishOptions holds the three settings, each optional: what a call leaves alone keeps the policy's value. The steps exist on a publisher whose options type is LapinPublishOptions. So the handler bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = LapinPublishOptions>, Slot> and still names no publisher type. The steps come from this crate's prelude, the one prelude a handler body imports besides the framework's. The values reach the frame as protocol fields, never as headers. The publish still leaves through the slot's own entry, with its codec and transforms. A test reads the options back with with_options on tb.out::<Slot>().

expiration gives one message a time to live; LapinPublish::expiration gives one to every message of a policy. A message nobody consumed within its TTL leaves the queue. The broker drops it, or dead-letters it where the queue has a dead-letter exchange. RabbitMQ expires a message when it reaches the head of its queue. A policy that sets no TTL sends messages that do not expire. AMQP counts the TTL in whole milliseconds, and a shorter non-zero TTL becomes one millisecond. A delivery reports it under EXPIRATION_HEADER in milliseconds.

persistent sets the delivery mode of one message; LapinPublish::persistent sets it for every message of a policy. A persistent message (delivery mode 2) on a durable queue survives a broker restart. A transient message (delivery mode 1) does not. The publish policies default to persistent. LapinRequest defaults to transient: a request nobody waits for after its timeout gains nothing from a restart.

priority sets the AMQP priority of one message; LapinPublish::priority sets it for every message of a policy. A policy that sets no priority sends none. RabbitMQ orders deliveries by priority only on a queue declared with x-max-priority, and a higher priority counts as that maximum. On any other queue the priority travels to the consumer and orders nothing. A delivery reports it under PRIORITY_HEADER as decimal digits, and the handler reads it like any other header. A delayed redelivery keeps the priority its original delivery reported.

A reading over 90 degrees raises an alert at priority 9, a warm one at the policy's 1. The alerts queue orders by priority, and its consumer pages someone for the urgent ones. LapinRequest, Request in the prelude, gives a handler a requester: it publishes a request over RabbitMQ direct reply-to and awaits the correlated reply. The handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply> and calls request with a message and a timeout. At startup the runtime pairs the policy into a LapinRequester. Each request goes out with reply-to set to the amq.rabbitmq.reply-to pseudo-queue and a generated correlation-id. The reply that carries that id resolves the call, and a reply with an id nobody waits for is dropped. No reply within the timeout fails the call with AmqpError::RequestTimeout. One task per requester reads the replies, started by its first request on the runtime the broker connected on. The request carries bytes, so the example encodes the question and decodes the answer with the core's JSON codec. The policy takes exchange, priority and expiration like a publish policy. Requests are transient by default, and persistent(true) makes them persistent. Direct reply-to is at-most-once: the reply state lives on the requester's channel on one node, and nothing is queued durably. A channel that drops loses the replies in flight, and the caller sees a timeout. The responder is any service that answers at the received reply-to with the same correlation-id, as DirectReplyTo does.

An order asks the inventory service whether its item is in stock. An order in stock is accepted, one out of stock is dropped, and no answer brings the order back. Macros Manual examples/lapin_request_request.rs /// Asks the inventory service whether `sku` is in stock, and waits two seconds at most. async fn in_stock( inventory: &impl RequestReply, sku: &str, ) -> Result<bool, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let request = JsonCodec.encode(&CheckStock { sku: sku.to_owned(), })?; let ask = OutgoingMessage::new("inventory.check", request.as_ref()); let reply = inventory.request(ask, Duration::from_secs(2)).await?; let stock: Stock = JsonCodec.decode(reply.payload())?; Ok(stock.available) } /// An order in stock is accepted and one out of stock is dropped. An inventory service that does /// not answer brings the order back. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn place_order(order: &Order, Out(inventory): Out<impl RequestReply>) -> HandlerOutcome { match in_stock(inventory, &order.sku).await { Ok(true) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Ok(false) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "inventory unavailable"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/lapin_request_request.rs /// Asks the inventory service whether `sku` is in stock, and waits two seconds at most. async fn in_stock( inventory: &impl RequestReply, sku: &str, ) -> Result<bool, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let request = JsonCodec.encode(&CheckStock { sku: sku.to_owned(), })?; let ask = OutgoingMessage::new("inventory.check", request.as_ref()); let reply = inventory.request(ask, Duration::from_secs(2)).await?; let stock: Stock = JsonCodec.decode(reply.payload())?; Ok(stock.available) } /// An order in stock is accepted and one out of stock is dropped. An inventory service that does /// not answer brings the order back. struct PlaceOrder; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for PlaceOrder where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: RequestReply>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match in_stock(outs.get(DefaultSlot), &order.sku).await { Ok(true) => Ok(()), Ok(false) => Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "inventory unavailable"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } } } The app mounts the requester's policy on the handler's slot. DirectReplyTo is a reply transform: it sends each reply to the address the request named in reply-to and echoes the request's correlation-id. It mounts on the reply position: .out_reply(policy).transform(DirectReplyTo). The handler is an ordinary reply handler and knows nothing about the requester. The transform names the destination of every reply, so it mounts only over a reply type that declares none. Over a type with its own #[outgoing(name = "..")] the mount does not compile. The name in the mount site's reply("..") is the fallback: a request without reply-to is answered there, and the generated AsyncAPI document reports it. A LapinRequest requester and a requester on another stack both name the reply address this way. With automatic recovery, the reply dispatcher resumes after Lapin restores its channel and direct reply-to consumer. Deadlines of requests already waiting for replies keep running during the outage; recovery does not restart them or replay their requests. A reply lost during a disconnect may therefore end in AmqpError::RequestTimeout.

The inventory service answers every stock check at the address the request named. A request without one is answered at inventory.check.unrouted. Macros Manual examples/lapin_request_direct_reply_to.rs /// The reply goes wherever the request asks, so its type declares no destination. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Stock { sku: String, available: bool, } #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("inventory.check"), reply("inventory.check.unrouted"))] async fn check(ask: &CheckStock) -> Stock { Stock { sku: ask.sku.clone(), available: ask.sku != "unobtainium", } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inventory", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(check) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(DirectReplyTo); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_request_direct_reply_to.rs /// The reply goes wherever the request asks, so its type declares no destination. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Stock { sku: String, available: bool, } struct Check; impl Handle<CheckStock, Stock> for Check { fn handle( &self, ask: &CheckStock, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Stock, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Stock { sku: ask.sku.clone(), available: ask.sku != "unobtainium", })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inventory", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { let check = subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("inventory.check"), Check); b.include(check.reply().to("inventory.check.unrouted").build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(DirectReplyTo); }, ) }

A handler's answer settles its AMQP delivery with a protocol frame: ack sends basic.ack, retry sends basic.reject with requeue, and drop sends basic.reject without it. The frame goes out on the channel the delivery arrived on, and the service publishes nothing. A requeued message goes back to its queue, which hands it out again with the redelivered flag set. The next delivery may reach this consumer or another consumer of the same queue. A handler reads the flag through the Redelivered key of the delivery context. A dropped message leaves the queue: RabbitMQ discards it, or routes it to the queue's dead-letter exchange. The crate settles with basic.reject and never with basic.nack. On one delivery the two frames do the same thing, but RabbitMQ counts a rejected delivery as spent and does not count a nacked one. So a handler that keeps asking for its message back runs down a quorum queue's delivery limit. A quorum queue stamps a returned message with the x-delivery-count header; a classic queue keeps no count, only the flag. A retry under a cap is a requeue too: the quorum queue counts it. A delayed retry travels as a copy through the queue's waiting queue. After a connection loss, a delivery's old acknowledgement belongs to the old channel and can fail even if the connection has recovered. RabbitMQ requeues unsettled messages from queues that survive the disconnect and may deliver them again. Do not treat reconnection as proof that the old delivery was settled; handlers must tolerate redelivery when recovery is enabled.

An order is requeued the first time it arrives and acknowledged when it comes back redelivered. An order without a SKU is dropped. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_outcomes.rs /// An order without a SKU is rejected for good. Any other order is requeued once, the first time /// it arrives, and acknowledged when the queue hands it out again marked redelivered. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.sku.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without a SKU, rejected"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !redelivered { tracing::info!(order.id, "stock not counted yet, back to the queue"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, "reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("stock", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(reserve); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_outcomes.rs /// An order without a SKU is rejected for good. Any other order is requeued once, the first time /// it arrives, and acknowledged when the queue hands it out again marked redelivered. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order, (), (), AmqpContext> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, AmqpContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let outcome = if order.sku.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without a SKU, rejected"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } else if !ctx.context(Redelivered) { tracing::info!(order.id, "stock not counted yet, back to the queue"); Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } else { tracing::info!(order.id, "reserved"); Ok(()) }; ready(outcome) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("stock", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Reserve).build()); }, ) }

dead_letter_exchange gives a queue its own route for the messages it rejects: the x-dead-letter-exchange argument. A drop settles with basic.reject without requeue, and the queue publishes the message to that exchange. The route belongs to the queue, so it takes every message the queue dead-letters, whatever the cause. Besides a rejection, RabbitMQ dead-letters a message whose TTL expired, one pushed out by a length limit, and one that spent a quorum queue's delivery limit. The message keeps its routing key, unless dead_letter_routing_key names another (x-dead-letter-routing-key). The dead-letter exchange routes like any other exchange: a queue bound to it under that key collects the messages. RabbitQuorumQueue takes the same two settings. Both settings are queue arguments. The queue gets them when the service declares it, with declare_topology(true) on the broker. A queue the operator provisions carries the arguments it was declared with. The dead_letter(name) step of the mount chain writes the same route from the registration: the default exchange, with name as the routing key. It is the step a classic queue takes from the retry steps.

An invoice with a negative amount is dropped. The queue dead-letters it to invoices.dlx, where a second subscription reads it from the bound queue. delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()) makes retry_after wait on the broker: the copy parks in a waiting queue under a per-message TTL. On a retry_after, the crate publishes the copy to the waiting queue with the delay as its expiration, then acknowledges the original. Both frames go out on one channel in that order, so a connection lost between them brings the original back rather than losing it. The waiting queue has no consumers. When the TTL fires, it dead-letters the copy back to the origin queue on the default exchange. The copy lives on the broker, so it survives a restart of the service. The waiting queue is <queue>.retry; Delay::dlx_ttl_named names another. The released copy is a new message to the server, and it carries x-ruststream-retry-count raised by one. A quorum queue counts the copy from zero, so a retry cap ends immediate retries only. A waiting queue releases expired messages only from its head, so a short delay waits behind a long one. Mixed delays take one waiting queue per delay class, or the delayed-message plugin. The waiting queue is infrastructure. With declare_topology(true) the service declares it: durable, dead-lettering to the origin queue. On a broker that declares nothing, the operator provisions it with those arguments. The subscription checks at startup that the waiting queue exists, and the service fails to start without it.

A shipment that arrives while the warehouse is closed waits a minute in shipments.retry. The released copy carries the retry count, and the shipment goes out. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_delay.rs /// A shipment that arrives while the warehouse is closed waits a minute in `shipments.retry`, on /// the broker. The copy it releases carries the retry count, and the shipment goes out. struct Dispatch; impl Handle<Shipment> for Dispatch { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "warehouse closed, waiting"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(WAIT))); } tracing::info!(shipment.id, "dispatched"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares its queues, `shipments.retry` included. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let shipments = RabbitQueue::new("shipments").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()); b.include(subscriber(shipments, Dispatch).build()); }) }

delivery_limit(n) sets a quorum queue's x-delivery-limit: how many times the queue returns a message before it carries it away. The argument counts returns, so the queue delivers a message n + 1 times: delivery_limit(4) delivers it five times. A quorum queue counts a delivery the handler rejected and a delivery whose consumer went away without settling it. Once the count passes the limit, the queue sends the message to its dead-letter exchange, or drops it when it has none. The server applies the limit itself: it holds while no service is running, and the service publishes nothing. A quorum queue without a limit of its own takes RabbitMQ's default of 20 returns. A returned message carries the queue's count in the x-delivery-count header. A registration states the same through the mount chain: max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(name). On a quorum queue the pair becomes an x-delivery-limit of n - 1 and a dead-letter route to the queue name, written over the descriptor's limit. The pair reaches the queue only when the service declares it, so the broker sets declare_topology(true). On a broker that declares nothing the subscription refuses to start, and so does half of the pair. out_retry(policy) does not compile on a quorum queue, because no copy leaves this process. A classic queue has no delivery limit, so max_attempts(n) is for a quorum queue only.

The provider refuses a charge every time. The queue delivers it five times and then moves it to charges.dlx, where a classic queue keeps it. Delay::plugin_dme hands a delayed copy to RabbitMQ's delayed-message-exchange plugin instead of a waiting queue. The crate publishes the copy to an x-delayed-message exchange with the delay in its x-delay header, then acknowledges the original. The plugin holds each message for its own delay and then routes it to the origin queue. So a short delay never waits behind a long one, and one exchange serves every delay. The exchange is <queue>.delay; Delay::plugin_dme_named names another, which several queues may share. The released copy carries x-ruststream-retry-count raised by one, as with a waiting queue. The backend sits behind the crate's plugin-dme feature, and the plugin has to be enabled on the server. With declare_topology(true) the service declares the exchange and binds the origin queue to it. On a broker that declares nothing, the operator provisions both, and the subscription checks at startup that the exchange exists.

Each reminder waits as long as it asks for. The in-process transport releases the copy like a waiting queue; the plugin's own release order shows only against a server with the plugin. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_plugin_dme.rs /// Each reminder waits as long as it asks, in the plugin's exchange `reminders.delay`. A short /// wait is released on time even while a long one is still held. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("reminders").delay(Delay::plugin_dme()))] async fn remind(reminder: &Reminder, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(reminder.after_secs)); } tracing::info!(reminder.id, "reminder sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares the delayed exchange; the plugin has to be enabled on the server. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reminders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(remind); }) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_plugin_dme.rs /// Each reminder waits as long as it asks, in the plugin's exchange `reminders.delay`. A short /// wait is released on time even while a long one is still held. struct Remind; impl Handle<Reminder> for Remind { fn handle( &self, reminder: &Reminder, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { let wait = Duration::from_secs(reminder.after_secs); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(wait))); } tracing::info!(reminder.id, "reminder sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The service declares the delayed exchange; the plugin has to be enabled on the server. let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reminders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let reminders = RabbitQueue::new("reminders").delay(Delay::plugin_dme()); b.include(subscriber(reminders, Remind).build()); }) }

max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(name) end a message that keeps failing, and RabbitMQ applies both itself. max_attempts(n) is how many deliveries one message gets, the first included. dead_letter(name) is where it goes when the queue carries it away. Each step becomes an argument of the queue, so the server moves the message and the service publishes nothing. Queue max_attempts(n) dead_letter(name) RabbitQuorumQueue x-delivery-limit of n - 1 dead-letter route to the queue name RabbitQueue refused at startup dead-letter route to the queue name a bare queue name refused at startup refused at startup A quorum queue counts the deliveries a message spends, so it takes the pair: the message that reaches the cap leaves for name. A classic queue counts nothing, so it has no cap; the service refuses to start with max_attempts(..) on one, and the error names the quorum queue. On a classic queue, dead_letter(name) takes the messages the handler drops. A bare queue name carries no queue arguments, so it takes neither step; the error names the descriptor to mount instead. The route is the queue's own, written as x-dead-letter-exchange (the default exchange) and x-dead-letter-routing-key (name), unless the descriptor names a dead-letter exchange of its own. The arguments reach the queue when the service declares it with declare_topology(true). A queue that already exists with other arguments is refused by the server, and the service fails to start with the queue and the arguments in the error. On a broker that declares nothing, a classic queue keeps the route its operator gave it, and a quorum queue refuses the pair. out_retry(policy) does not compile on either queue: no copy leaves this process.

retry_after(delay) asks for a redelivery no sooner than delay, for a message that is not ready yet. AMQP has no per-message delay, so the queue takes one with delay. On a retry_after, the crate publishes a copy to the queue's waiting queue and acknowledges the delivery. The waiting queue releases the copy back to the queue once the delay is up. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER raised by one, and it lives on the broker, so a service that stops during the delay does not lose it. On a queue without a delay, retry_after requeues the delivery at once and drops the delay; the runtime logs a warning.

The first delivery finds the payment unsettled and asks for the refund again in 30 seconds. The waiting queue refunds.retry holds the copy, which comes back with the retry count, and the refund goes through. Macros Manual examples/lapin_settlement_retry_after.rs /// The first delivery finds the payment unsettled and asks for the refund again in 30 seconds. /// The copy that comes back carries the retry count, and the refund goes through. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("refunds").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()))] async fn issue_refund(refund: &Refund, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(refund.id, "payment not settled yet"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(refund.id, "refunded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true), |b| { b.include(issue_refund); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_settlement_retry_after.rs /// The first delivery finds the payment unsettled and asks for the refund again in 30 seconds. /// The copy that comes back carries the retry count, and the refund goes through. struct IssueRefund; impl Handle<Refund> for IssueRefund { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).is_none() { tracing::info!(refund.id, "payment not settled yet"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(refund.id, "refunded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true), |b| { b.include( subscriber( RabbitQueue::new("refunds").delay(Delay::dlx_ttl()), IssueRefund, ) .build(), ); }, ) }

A queue name in #[subscriber] consumes that existing queue as a classic queue; a descriptor carries every other setting. One subscription consumes one queue. #[subscriber("orders")] consumes the queue orders with the defaults of RabbitQueue: a durable classic queue, the broker's prefetch and no bindings. The queue has to exist on the server, unless the broker declares the topology. A message reaches it through the default exchange, which routes on the queue's name, or through an exchange the queue is bound to. RabbitMQ has two queue types, and the type is fixed when the queue is created. The type decides what a retry does, so each type has a descriptor of its own: Descriptor Queue A retry is RabbitQueue classic, on one node a requeue, with no count and no cap RabbitQuorumQueue quorum, replicated counted by the server, which ends a message that spent its deliveries A bare queue name carries no queue arguments, so it takes none of the retry steps: a registration that declares one names its queue with a descriptor. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument, and every one of its steps returns the descriptor. The manual form passes the name or the descriptor to subscriber(source, body). Several instances of a service share one queue, and each message goes to one of them. The handler's outcome is a protocol frame: an ack removes the message, and a retry or a drop rejects it, as the Settlement pages show. With automatic recovery enabled, a subscription waits while Lapin restores its channel and consumer, then resumes through the same handle. Unsettled deliveries may be redelivered after an outage, so handlers must tolerate duplicates. When retries run out, the stream yields a consume error and ends. Recovery is disabled by default.

An order with items is acknowledged; an empty order is dropped. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_queue.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.items == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "empty order dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_queue.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.items == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "empty order dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.items, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build()); }, ) }

argument and arguments pass any x- declaration argument the descriptor does not model, such as a TTL or a length limit, verbatim. A queue declaration carries a table of arguments, and RabbitMQ reads queue features from it: x-message-ttl, x-max-length, x-overflow, x-single-active-consumer and more. argument(name, value) adds one entry, and arguments(table) replaces the whole table. The value is an AMQPValue and the table a FieldTable, both re-exported from lapin. A name is at most 255 bytes, the protocol's limit for a field name. The settings the descriptor models, such as the dead-letter exchange and the queue type, travel in the same table, so they are written with their own steps. The arguments reach the server in the queue's declaration, so they take effect where the broker declares the topology. A queue keeps the arguments it was first declared with. A declaration with other arguments is refused with PRECONDITION_FAILED, and startup fails with AmqpError::Declare; the in-process transport refuses it the same way. What an argument does to the messages, such as a TTL that expires them, is the server's work and shows only against a server.

Notifications expire after a minute, and the queue holds at most ten thousand of them. The macro form adds the arguments one by one; the manual form builds the table. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_arguments.rs /// A notification older than a minute is no longer worth sending, and the queue keeps at most /// ten thousand of them. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("notifications") .argument("x-message-ttl", AMQPValue::LongLongInt(60_000)) .argument("x-max-length", AMQPValue::LongLongInt(10_000)))] async fn notify(notification: &Notification) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(notification.user, "notification sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_arguments.rs struct Notify; impl Handle<Notification> for Notify { fn handle( &self, notification: &Notification, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(notification.user, "notification sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// A notification older than a minute is no longer worth sending, and the queue keeps at most /// ten thousand of them. fn notifications() -> RabbitQueue { let mut arguments = FieldTable::default(); arguments.insert("x-message-ttl".into(), AMQPValue::LongLongInt(60_000)); arguments.insert("x-max-length".into(), AMQPValue::LongLongInt(10_000)); RabbitQueue::new("notifications").arguments(arguments) }

A slice handler gets a batch assembled on the client, up to the mount site's size or until batch_wait (50 ms) passes since the first delivery. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. AMQP pushes one delivery at a time, so the subscription collects deliveries into a batch on the client. A batch closes when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first delivery, 50 ms by default. A raised wait gives fuller batches on a sparse queue; a lowered one hands a short batch over sooner. The server sends no more than the prefetch window, so a window below n keeps every batch below n. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>: Ok(()) acknowledges the batch, and Err(outcomes) settles delivery i with outcome i. workers(n) keeps up to n batches in flight at once.

Payments settle up to 32 at a time, and a batch that does not fill closes 200 ms after its first payment. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_batches.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Settles up to 32 payments in one call; a batch that does not fill closes 200 ms after its /// first payment arrived. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments") .prefetch(nonzero!(64)) .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)))] async fn settle(payments: &[Payment]) -> HandlerOutcome { let cents: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), cents, "payments settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(settle.batch(nonzero!(32))); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_batches.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// Settles a batch of payments; `Ok` acknowledges the whole batch. struct Settle; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Settle { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let cents: u64 = payments.iter().map(|payment| payment.cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = payments.len(), cents, "payments settled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { // Up to 32 payments per call; a batch that does not fill closes 200 ms after its // first payment arrived. let payments = RabbitQueue::new("payments") .prefetch(nonzero!(64)) .batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)); b.include(subscriber(payments, Settle).batch(nonzero!(32)).build()); }, ) }

workers(n, by_key) keeps deliveries that share the amqp-partition-key header on one lane, in order, while other keys run in parallel. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes over one queue. The lane of a delivery is picked by a hash of its partition key, so deliveries with one key run one after another, in queue order. Deliveries with different keys run at once on different lanes. A delivery without a key goes to the next lane in rotation. On RabbitMQ the key is the header PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, amqp-partition-key. AMQP gives the header no meaning: it is a convention between the publisher, which sets it, and this crate, which reads it back. A service that publishes to a keyed queue sets the header on each message, such as the tenant or the account the message belongs to. The lanes order work inside one service instance. Spreading a stream over several queues by key is the consistent-hash exchange, which the server runs. The manual form writes the lanes as .workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

Orders of one tenant run in order on one lane, and different tenants run side by side. prefetch caps unacknowledged deliveries per subscription on the broker or one descriptor; unset, the server applies no limit. The server pushes deliveries to a consumer without waiting to be asked. The prefetch window (basic.qos) is how many deliveries it may have out to one subscription before the service settles some of them. So the window is the back-pressure between a queue and a service: a slow handler holds the rest of the queue on the server, where other instances can take it. LapinBroker::prefetch sets the window for every subscription of the broker. RabbitQueue::prefetch and RabbitQuorumQueue::prefetch set it for one subscription and take precedence. The count is a NonZeroU16, because AMQP reads a window of 0 as no limit. A subscription with neither setting has no window, and the server pushes it the whole queue. A batch handler needs a window of at least its batch size, or its batches stay short. The window is the server's: the in-process transport has none and hands a subscription everything its queue holds. A test of the window runs against a server with TestApp::start_live.

RabbitQueue consumes a classic queue: its durability, exclusivity, auto-delete, bindings and the settings shared with quorum queues. RabbitQueue::new names the queue. Three settings belong to the classic queue alone: Setting Default What it does durable true the queue survives a broker restart exclusive false the queue belongs to the connection that declared it and goes with it auto_delete false the server deletes the queue once its last consumer leaves RabbitMQ 4 refuses a transient queue that other connections may share, so durable(false) comes with exclusive(true). An exclusive queue suits a per-instance feed, such as a cache that every instance refreshes from a fanout exchange. The other settings are shared with RabbitQuorumQueue: bind and bind_with join the queue to exchanges, dead_letter_exchange and dead_letter_routing_key give it a route for rejected messages, prefetch and batch_wait shape its consumption, delay parks delayed retries on the server, and argument passes anything else the queue declaration takes. Bindings, the dead-letter route and the arguments reach the server when the broker declares the topology. A classic queue keeps no count of a message's deliveries. A retry puts the message back on the queue, and its next delivery carries the redelivered flag, which a handler reads through the Redelivered key. Of the retry steps at the mount site, a classic queue takes dead_letter(name), which becomes its dead-letter route. It has no cap, so max_attempts(n) stops the service at startup; a quorum queue takes it.

The order queue is bound to a topic exchange and dead-letters to orders.failed; an order that fails once is placed on its redelivery. The price queue belongs to this instance alone. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_rabbit_queue.rs /// A durable queue fed by the topic exchange `events`; a dropped order leaves through /// `orders.failed`. A delivery the server already handed out once is placed on its second try. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*") .dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed"))] async fn place(order: &Order, Ctx(redelivered): Ctx<Redelivered>) -> HandlerOutcome { if !redelivered && order.flaky { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, redelivered, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A queue of this instance alone: it lives as long as the connection that declared it. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("prices.instance-a") .durable(false) .exclusive(true) .auto_delete(true) .bind(RabbitExchange::fanout("prices"), ""))] async fn refresh(price: &Price) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(price.sku, price.cents, "price cached"); if !redelivered && order.flaky { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, redelivered, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// A durable queue fed by the topic exchange `events`; a dropped order leaves through /// `orders.failed`. fn orders() -> RabbitQueue { RabbitQueue::new("orders") .bind(RabbitExchange::topic("events"), "order.*") .dead_letter_exchange("orders.failed") } struct Refresh; RabbitQuorumQueue consumes a replicated quorum queue, which is always durable and counts the deliveries each message spends. A quorum queue keeps its messages on several nodes through Raft, so it survives the loss of a node. It is durable, shared and permanent by definition. So the descriptor has no durable, exclusive or auto_delete step, and a quorum queue that contradicts its type does not compile. Every shared setting of RabbitQueue is on it too. The server counts each delivery of a message, and a retry spends one. A quorum delivery reports its count, where a classic delivery reports only the redelivered flag. Past the queue's delivery limit the server takes the message off the queue: it dead-letters the message when the queue has a dead-letter exchange, and drops it otherwise. RabbitMQ 4 gives a quorum queue a limit of 20 when it names none, so a message that keeps failing gets 21 deliveries. delivery_limit sets another limit; max_attempts with dead_letter at the mount site sets it from the registration. The queue type is part of the declaration, so a quorum queue is created by an operator or by a broker that declares the topology. A quorum queue refuses some classic arguments: a declaration with x-max-priority fails with AmqpError::Declare.

A reservation waits for stock; one that never fits ends after the queue's default delivery limit. Macros Manual examples/lapin_subscriptions_quorum.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// A reservation waits for stock; the queue gives up on one after its delivery limit. #[subscriber(RabbitQuorumQueue::new("reservations"))] async fn reserve(reservation: &Reservation) -> HandlerOutcome { if !reservation.in_stock { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(reservation.id, "reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reservations", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(reserve); }) } examples/manual/lapin_subscriptions_quorum.rs use ruststream_lapin::prelude::*; /// A reservation waits for stock; the queue gives up on one after its delivery limit. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Reservation> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, reservation: &Reservation, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !reservation.in_stock { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(reservation.id, "reserved"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reservations", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let reservations = RabbitQuorumQueue::new("reservations"); b.include(subscriber(reservations, Reserve).build()); }) }

TestApp::start runs the production app on LapinBroker in process, with exchanges, bindings, requeues, quorum counts and reply-to. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<LapinBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process transport has no settings of its own. It reads the broker's: declare_topology decides whether a subscription declares its queue, as on the server. A publish is framed by the same conversion a publish to the server goes through. The transport keeps RabbitMQ's semantics. The default exchange and the direct, topic, fanout and headers exchanges route through the bindings the descriptors declare. Consumers of one queue compete for its messages, and a requeue puts a message back in its queue. A queue keeps what reaches it from its first subscription on, until an auto-delete queue loses its last consumer. A consumer that closes returns what it took and left unsettled. A quorum queue counts deliveries and dead-letters a spent one through its route. A waiting queue releases a delayed copy, and direct reply-to gives every request an address of its own. The transport refuses what the server refuses, with the same error. That covers a name over 255 bytes, a header the frame cannot carry, and a body over the server's default max_message_size of 16 MiB. It covers the declarations the server refuses: a transient queue that is not exclusive, a binding on the default exchange, a queue declared again with other settings, a quorum queue with a priority. A delivery settled after its connection closed reports the closed channel. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply or a slot publish included. The assertions that follow read finished state. What only a server has is for a live test: the prefetch window, publisher confirms, the atomicity of a server transaction, a plugin exchange's routing, a queue two connections share, and a topology the service finds without declaring it.

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running RabbitMQ, one subscription per queue, for what only a server has. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription consumes from the server. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process transport leaves to the server: the prefetch window, publisher confirms, the atomicity of a server transaction, a plugin exchange's routing, and a topology the service finds without declaring it. A live test keeps one subscription per queue. The server picks which consumer of a queue takes a message, so a test with two subscriptions of one queue stops at the first publish and names the queue. A server keeps what earlier runs left in it. In the example the service declares its queue with declare_topology, and the queue is exclusive: it lives as long as the test's connection. live::url is the repository's test helper: it returns the server's address from AMQP_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

A handler bounded Out<impl TransactionalPublisher> opens a transaction scope with begin, publishes through it, and ends it with commit or abort. The scope's publishes become visible together at commit, and abort discards them. The handler names the capability, TransactionalPublisher, and the mount site names the policy that provides it. ConfirmsPublish, TransactionalPublish in the prelude, buffers in the client and commits by awaiting a broker confirm for every message. ServerTxPublish runs an AMQP channel transaction on the server. LapinPublish pairs into a publisher with no transaction surface, so a transactional handler mounted with it does not compile. A publisher runs one such transaction at a time. A second begin while one is open, or a commit or abort with none open, fails with AmqpError::Transaction and leaves the open transaction as it was. A publisher is a shared handle: every clone uses one channel and one transaction state. Several independent groups of messages in one handler take the owned kind, ConfirmsTransaction.

An order ships one message per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts the transaction, and the shipments already published are discarded. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_scope.rs /// One shipment per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts it, and the shipments /// already published are discarded with it. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(scope) = shipments.begin().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an item without a name, nothing shipped"); return match scope.abort().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), }; } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if scope.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if scope.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_scope.rs /// One shipment per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts it, and the shipments /// already published are discarded with it. struct Ship; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Ship where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let scope = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .begin() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an item without a name, nothing shipped"); scope.abort().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if scope.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } scope.commit().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_scope.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { // The confirms policy; `LapinPublish::default().server_tx()` is the other one. b.include(ship) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_scope.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { // The confirms policy; `LapinPublish::default().server_tx()` is the other one. b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Ship).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) }

ConfirmsPublish, TransactionalPublish in the prelude, is the publish policy whose every publish resolves once the broker has confirmed the message. LapinPublish::confirms reaches it with the same settings: exchange and property defaults. It pairs into a ConfirmsPublisher with a confirm channel of its own. A message the broker refuses fails the publish, and the handler decides what follows. RabbitMQ confirms a message once it has routed it, and a message that matches no queue is confirmed and dropped. So a confirm says the broker took the message, not that a queue holds it. Inside a transaction the publisher buffers in the client. commit publishes the buffer in order and resolves once every message is confirmed, and abort discards the buffer without touching the broker. A failed commit loses the buffer, and the delivery's redelivery is the way to recover. The policy offers the borrowed kind of the transaction scope and the owned kind of ConfirmsTransaction.

A payment is acknowledged once the broker has confirmed its receipt. A receipt the broker refused brings the payment back. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_confirms.rs /// The payment is acknowledged once the broker has confirmed its receipt. A receipt the broker /// refused brings the payment back. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments"))] async fn settle(payment: &Payment, Out(receipts): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let receipt = Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, }; if let Err(err) = receipts.message(&receipt).publish().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "receipt not confirmed"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.cents, "payment settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(settle) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_confirms.rs /// The payment is acknowledged once the broker has confirmed its receipt. A receipt the broker /// refused brings the payment back. struct Settle; impl<Egress> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Settle where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let receipt = Receipt { payment_id: payment.id, }; let receipts = outs.get(DefaultSlot); if let Err(err) = receipts.message(&receipt).publish().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "receipt not confirmed"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(payment.id, payment.cents, "payment settled"); Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("payments"), Settle).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }) }

ConfirmsTransaction is an owned confirm transaction: a value that holds its own publish buffer. A handler bounded Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Slot> opens one with transaction() on its slot, and every call opens another. Any number can be open on one publisher, and settling one never touches another. The publisher keeps publishing directly while they are open. commit publishes the buffer in order and awaits every confirm, and abort discards it without touching the broker. Both consume the value, so a double commit or a publish after settling does not compile. A failed commit loses the buffer, and the delivery's redelivery is the way to recover. Only ConfirmsPublish offers the owned kind.

The shipment and the audit record of an order go out in two transactions. An order out of stock aborts the shipment and still commits its audit record. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_owned.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment, AuditRecord)] struct Records; /// The shipment and the audit record go out in two transactions. The shipment waits in its own /// buffer while the stock is checked: an order out of stock aborts it and still commits its audit /// record. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"))] async fn record( order: &Order, Out(records): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Records>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let (Ok(mut shipment), Ok(mut audit)) = (records.transaction().await, records.transaction().await) else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let shipped = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if shipment.message(&shipped).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } let settled = if order.in_stock { shipment.commit().await } else { shipment.abort().await }; if settled.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } let entry = AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, shipped: order.in_stock, }; if audit.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(record) .out(Records, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_owned.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment, AuditRecord)] struct Records; /// The shipment and the audit record go out in two transactions. The shipment waits in its own /// buffer while the stock is checked: an order out of stock aborts it and still commits its audit /// record. struct Record; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Record where Egress: OutEntry<Records, Wire: OwnedTransactions>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let records = outs.get(Records); let (Ok(mut shipment), Ok(mut audit)) = (records.transaction().await, records.transaction().await) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let shipped = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; if shipment.message(&shipped).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } let settled = if order.in_stock { shipment.commit().await } else { shipment.abort().await }; if settled.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } let entry = AuditRecord { order_id: order.id, shipped: order.in_stock, }; if audit.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("orders"), Record).build()) .out(Records, TransactionalPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) }

ServerTxPublish is the publish policy backed by AMQP channel transactions: tx.select, tx.commit and tx.rollback. LapinPublish::server_tx reaches it with the same settings. It pairs into a ServerTxPublisher on a channel of its own. Between begin and commit the messages wait on the broker inside the channel transaction, and they become visible together at commit. abort rolls them back on the server. Each commit is a synchronous round trip, which makes the policy slower than ConfirmsPublish. Outside a transaction a publish behaves like a fire-and-forget one. The transaction is the channel's state, so the policy offers only the borrowed kind of the transaction scope. Server transactions require auto_recover(false), which is the default. Lapin cannot restore a transaction's state after a disconnect, so pairing this policy with auto_recover(true) fails with AmqpError::InvalidOptions before it is used. Direct publish, begin, commit and abort calls also reject that combination. Use publisher confirms when enabling connection recovery.

The debit and the credit of a transfer are published in one server transaction. A frozen account rolls it back, and the debit already sent is discarded on the broker. Macros Manual examples/lapin_transactions_server_tx.rs /// The debit and the credit of a transfer are published in one server transaction. A frozen /// account rolls it back, and the debit already sent is discarded on the broker. #[subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("transfers"))] async fn book( transfer: &Transfer, Out(ledger): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(scope) = ledger.begin().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let legs = [ (transfer.from, -transfer.cents), (transfer.to, transfer.cents), ]; for (account, cents) in legs { if account == FROZEN { tracing::warn!(account, "frozen account, transfer rolled back"); return match scope.abort().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), }; } if scope .message(&Entry { account, cents }) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if scope.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(book) .out(DefaultSlot, ServerTxPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) } examples/manual/lapin_transactions_server_tx.rs /// The debit and the credit of a transfer are published in one server transaction. A frozen /// account rolls it back, and the debit already sent is discarded on the broker. struct Book; impl<Egress> Handle<Transfer, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Book where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, transfer: &Transfer, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let scope = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .begin() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; let legs = [ (transfer.from, -transfer.cents), (transfer.to, transfer.cents), ]; for (account, cents) in legs { if account == FROZEN { tracing::warn!(account, "frozen account, transfer rolled back"); scope.abort().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if scope .message(&Entry { account, cents }) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } scope.commit().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RabbitQueue::new("transfers"), Book).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, ServerTxPublish::default()) .build(); }, ) }
Это руководство устанавливает ruststream-lapin, запускает локальный RabbitMQ и первый сервис на нём.

Для сборки не нужно ничего, кроме Cargo. Фича testing брокера добавляет RabbitMQ внутри процесса, на котором работают тесты. Для разработки достаточно одного узла RabbitMQ с веб-интерфейсом управления: compose.yaml services: rabbitmq: image: rabbitmq:4-management-alpine ports: - "127.0.0.1:5672:5672" - "127.0.0.1:15672:15672" docker compose up -d Брокер слушает localhost:5672. Веб-интерфейс управления открывается по адресу http://localhost:15672, пользователь guest, пароль guest. RabbitMQ пускает учётную запись guest только с локального адреса, поэтому порты опубликованы на 127.0.0.1.

Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true), |b| { b.include(take_order); }, ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672").declare_topology(true), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", TakeOrder).build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order читает заказы в JSON из очереди orders. Заказ с суммой он подтверждает, а заказ без суммы отбрасывает. LapinBroker::new принимает URI соединения и только запоминает его. Соединение открывается при запуске сервиса. declare_topology(true) разрешает сервису объявить очереди, которые он читает, поэтому сервис запускается и на пустом RabbitMQ. #[ruststream::app] превращает app в main. В ручной форме то же делает run_main. Запустите сервис: cargo run -- run Опубликуйте заказ из другого терминала утилитой rabbitmqadmin, которая входит в образ: docker compose exec rabbitmq rabbitmqadmin publish message \ --routing-key orders --payload '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' Сообщение уходит в обменник по умолчанию, а он доставляет его в очередь, имя которой совпадает с ключом маршрутизации. Сервис пишет в журнал order taken с номером заказа. То же сообщение можно опубликовать со страницы очереди orders в веб-интерфейсе управления. Ctrl+C останавливает сервис. Сервис умеет и описать себя: cargo run -- asyncapi gen Команда выводит документ AsyncAPI сервиса: сервер, канал orders и сообщение Order. cargo generate создаёт такой же сервис с роутером и ответом: cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream-lapin templates/amqp-queue --name my-service Шаблон templates/amqp-topic вместо этого начинает с обменника типа topic.
